passage: The laptop died on Friday, the exchange-programme essay was due on Monday, and outside the hostel a Holi party was thumping with drums and a loudspeaker. Noor sat on the common-room floor with a notebook and a pencil and made one rule: write, don't fix. For forty minutes she scribbled everything: the grandmother who taught her to read Urdu, the bus conductor in Pune who corrected her Marathi, why Istanbul, a half-joke about tea. When a sentence came out clumsy, she drew an arrow and kept going. Four messy pages. Then she shut the notebook, went out, got pink powder in her hair, and didn't look at it again that day. On Sunday morning, in the quiet, she read it with a red pen as if a stranger had written it. The tea joke went. The bus conductor moved to the top. Two pages became one. At noon she typed it on Thomas's laptop. Thomas read it and said, "This sounds like you, only sharper."

qa.q: What rule did Noor make for writing the first draft?
qa.a: Write, don't fix.

qa.q: Why did Noor need the "write, don't fix" rule?
qa.a: She was probably afraid of getting stuck on a blank page, or of polishing each sentence while the deadline and the noise pressed in, so the rule let her keep going.

qa.q: Why did leaving the draft until Sunday help?
qa.a: Reading it the next morning as if a stranger had written it let her see clearly what to cut and move, so two pages became one sharper page.

qa.q: How does Thomas see the final essay?
qa.a: Thomas is impressed, saying it sounds like Noor, only sharper.

grounding: Illustrates a writer who drafts roughly without judging, leaves it overnight and then edits with fresh eyes, despite a broken laptop and a noisy hostel.

passage: Looking back, the message wasn't even long, but it ate my whole Tuesday. I'm Keerthana, and I coordinate transport for our school. Imran, who was organising annual day, sent this at 7 a.m.: "Hi, so annual day, you know how last year the buses were late and parents were upset, and this year the venue is the new auditorium which is further, and I was thinking about timing, maybe 5, maybe 5:30, principal hasn't confirmed, anyway the parents, can you see about it? Thanks!!" See about what? Buses? Parking? A notice? I read it four times on the staffroom sofa. I didn't want to look slow by asking. By lunch I guessed buses and booked three. At four, Imran called, puzzled. He'd only wanted to know how many parents needed a lift. Cancelling took an hour and an awkward call. The confusion was in his message, but the extra work had landed on me.

qa.q: How many buses did Keerthana book?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel reading the message on the staffroom sofa?
qa.a: Keerthana was confused and a bit anxious, reading it four times and not wanting to look slow by asking.

qa.q: What could Imran have written to save Keerthana's Tuesday?
qa.a: One clear line first, such as "Can you find out how many parents need a lift to the new auditorium, by Friday?", before any background.

qa.q: How did Imran see the situation when he called at four?
qa.a: Imran was puzzled by the buses, since the message seemed clear to him; he didn't realise the real question was buried in the ramble.

grounding: Shows a busy colleague who cannot tell what a rambling message wants, guesses wrongly, and ends up doing the work the unclear writing created.

passage: Last month I wrote the most useful email of my job so far, and it was also the shortest. I'm Raghav, and I handle supplies for our twelve bakery outlets. The flour supplier was changing on 1 March. My first draft opened with three paragraphs of background: the old supplier's delays, the tasting we'd done, my views on the new packaging. I read it aloud at my desk and got bored of my own voice halfway through. So I cut. The final version began: "From 1 March, flour comes from a new supplier. You need to do one thing." Then: "Deliveries arrive Tuesday and Friday before 7 a.m., not daily." Then: "Please send me your weekly flour quantity by 24 February." One short paragraph of background came last. The email shrank by about a third, and every line had a job. By the 24th, eleven outlets had replied. Gopika, my manager, forwarded it to the other region with one line: "Write like this."

qa.q: By what date did Raghav ask outlets to send their weekly flour quantity?
qa.a: By 24 February.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel reading the first draft aloud?
qa.a: Raghav felt bored by it, which was the signal to cut; afterwards Raghav seems quietly proud of the short version.

qa.q: Which changes made the final email work?
qa.a: The point came first, the sentences were short, the dates and days were exact, and it ended with one clear action and a deadline.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Raghav's email?
qa.a: Gopika sees it as a model and forwards it to the other region with "Write like this".

grounding: Illustrates a writer who puts the point first, uses short sentences with exact dates, ends with the action needed, and improves the draft by reading it aloud and cutting.

subtype: Fear of standing before the class [Actor]
passage: I'm Keerthana. In class five, Miss Ritu asked me to read my rain story aloud to the class. I stood up and my heart banged so hard I thought everyone could hear it. My mouth went dry like chalk. I looked at the page and the words swam. I read the first line, then lost my place, and somebody at the back giggled. I sat down with my face burning, sure the whole class would remember it forever. Miss Ritu didn't make me finish. That week she let me read the story just to her, at lunch. Then to her and my friend Anu. Then to four people on the steps. The next month I read a new story to the whole class. My heart still banged, but I got to the end.

qa.q: What story did Keerthana have to read aloud?
qa.a: The rain story.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel sitting down after the giggle?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and scared, face burning, sure the whole class would remember it forever.

qa.q: What did Miss Ritu do that made reading aloud less frightening?
qa.a: She let Keerthana practise in small, safe steps, first to her alone, then with Anu, then to four people, before the whole class.

qa.q: How might Miss Ritu have felt watching Keerthana sit down?
qa.a: Miss Ritu was probably concerned and kind, which is why she didn't force Keerthana to finish and planned small practice sessions instead.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild whose heart races and mouth goes dry reading in front of the class, and who grows braver through gentle practice in small groups.

passage: At the district science centre's student day, Ritu's turn came after lunch, when the hall was warm and sleepy. Her topic was solar cookers, and she had twelve slides crowded with full sentences. She stood half-turned to the screen and read: "A solar cooker is a device which uses the energy of direct sunlight to heat and cook food." Click. Next slide. Read. She didn't look at the audience once; looking at them made her throat close. From the third row, Reena watched a father check his phone, two boys whisper, a grandmother nod off. Ritu finished and got polite clapping. Outside, by the water cooler, Reena said carefully, "The pictures were great. But you read every word. People could've read it themselves." Ritu's face went tight. "If I look away from the screen, I'll forget everything." "Then put three words on each slide," Reena said, "and look at me. I'll nod." Ritu said nothing, but she didn't walk away.

qa.q: How many slides did Ritu have?
qa.a: Twelve slides.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Reena mentioned reading every word?
qa.a: Ritu felt stung and defensive, her face going tight, because reading was how she coped with her fear of forgetting.

qa.q: What small step did Reena suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Put three words on each slide and look at Reena, so Ritu has a prompt but talks to people, with a friendly nodding face to steady her.

qa.q: What was the talk like for the audience, as Reena saw it?
qa.a: They drifted away: a father checked his phone, two boys whispered and a grandmother nodded off, since everything was already written on the screen.

grounding: Shows a teenager who reads each slide word for word to cope with nerves and loses the audience, who could have read it themselves.

passage: At the agricultural college in Hassan, Dhruv's seminar on drip irrigation was the last of the afternoon, with twenty classmates and three farmers from the demonstration plot on the benches. Halfway through, he dropped the wooden pointer with a clatter, said "drop irrigation" instead of "drip", and lost his place for what felt like a full minute. His ears burned. He finished, sat down and replayed it: the clatter, the word, the silence. Everyone must think he was a fool. On the bus home he finally asked Raghav, "How bad was the pointer thing?" Raghav looked blank. "What pointer thing?" "I dropped it. And said drop irrigation." "Did you? I was busy worrying about my own slides. The tank diagram was good, though. That old farmer asked you about the pipes after, na?" Dhruv stared out at the coconut groves. The farmer had asked. Nobody had asked about the pointer.

qa.q: What did Dhruv say instead of "drip irrigation"?
qa.a: "Drop irrigation".

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel after sitting down?
qa.a: Dhruv was embarrassed and anxious, ears burning, replaying the stumble and sure everyone thought he was a fool.

qa.q: What could Dhruv remind himself before his next seminar?
qa.a: That listeners notice far less than he fears, as Raghav's blank look showed, and that they remember the useful parts like the tank diagram.

qa.q: How did Raghav experience Dhruv's seminar?
qa.a: Raghav barely noticed the stumble, being busy worrying about his own slides, and remembered the good tank diagram and the farmer's question instead.

grounding: Shows a student sure that every small stumble in his seminar was noticed, while the audience was mostly thinking about itself.

passage: "Ganga, you asked how the conference talk went. I'm Vijay, and honestly, the first minute was the worst minute of my life. My voice shook so much I could hear it through the speakers. I was sure a hundred people were thinking, who let this boy on stage? Then I noticed a woman in the second row, a stranger, grey kurta, notebook open. Every time I finished a sentence, she nodded. Just a small nod. So I started talking to her. By slide four my voice had stopped wobbling. Afterwards she found me at the tea counter and said, 'At my first talk my hands shook so much I dropped the clicker. I was cheering for you the whole time.' I couldn't believe it. I'd been bracing for judgment, and the room had been rooting for me. Now, when someone else is nervous up there, I'm the one in the second row, nodding."

qa.q: Where was the woman who nodded sitting?
qa.a: In the second row.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel during the first minute of the talk?
qa.a: He was terrified, his voice shaking through the speakers, sure a hundred people were judging him.

qa.q: Why did the woman's small nod help so much?
qa.a: It gave Vijay one friendly face to speak to, which steadied him, and showed that the audience was on his side.

qa.q: How did the woman in the grey kurta see Vijay's nerves?
qa.a: She felt sympathy, remembering her own shaking hands at her first talk, and was quietly cheering for him.

grounding: Shows a nervous speaker who fears judgment but is steadied by an audience member's sympathetic, attentive nodding.

passage: At the NGO's quarterly volunteer meeting in a Chennai school hall, Ankita sat in the fourth row with a notebook, determined to follow Payal's report on the reading programme. Slide one: enrolment by ward. Slide two: enrolment by age. Slide three: attendance by month, by ward, by age. Payal talked fast, pointing at columns. By slide nine Ankita had stopped writing. By slide fifteen she was wondering whether the canteen had idlis left, and felt guilty about it. Around her, two volunteers were scrolling their phones and the man beside her was drawing boxes in the margin. Then, near the end, almost as an aside, Payal said, "Oh, and Arif, eight, read the number on his bus by himself last week." The whole room looked up. Walking out, Ankita tried to recall a single figure from the thirty slides and couldn't. But that night she told her flatmate about Arif and the bus.

qa.q: What did Arif do by himself last week?
qa.a: He read the number on his bus.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel by slide fifteen?
qa.a: Ankita was bored and a little guilty for drifting off to thoughts of idlis, despite meaning to follow closely.

qa.q: What could Payal change in the next report?
qa.a: Lead with one clear message and a story like Arif's, then show just a few key figures that support it, instead of thirty slides of columns.

qa.q: What might Payal have hoped the thirty slides would show?
qa.a: Payal probably wanted to prove how much work and progress the programme had made, and may not have realised the room stopped following.

grounding: Shows a listener who stops following a report full of detail with no clear message, and remembers only the one story that made sense.

passage: "Preeti, you asked how I stayed calm in front of the town council. I'm Nilesh, and it wasn't nerves of steel. It was homework. First, I wrote my message on a card in one sentence: this bus shelter keeps people dry and costs less to repair. Everything else had to serve that line. Then I rehearsed aloud three times, once to my mother while she chopped onions, which is a tough audience. My slides were six photos and almost no words. On the day, one councillor folded his arms and asked about drainage costs, in a tone that said young engineers know nothing. I didn't know the exact figure. So I said, 'I don't know yet. I'll send it by Friday.' He blinked, and the room relaxed. I sent it on Thursday. Pretending to know would have made me shake. Saying I didn't know made me steady."

qa.q: How many times did Nilesh rehearse aloud?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when admitting to not knowing the drainage figure?
qa.a: Nilesh felt steady and calm, because honesty removed the pressure of pretending, which Nilesh says would have caused the shaking.

qa.q: Which parts of Nilesh's preparation were most steadying?
qa.a: A one-sentence main message, rehearsing aloud, light photo slides, and being ready to say "I don't know yet" and follow up.

qa.q: How might the councillor with folded arms have felt about the honest answer?
qa.a: The councillor seemed ready to catch a young engineer out, so the plain "I don't know yet" and a promised date took the edge off his doubt.

grounding: Illustrates a presenter steadied by a clear main message, rehearsal aloud, light slides and an honest admission of not knowing yet when asked a hard question.

passage:
"No, Simran, not like that! The bunny ear goes round the tree!"
"What tree?"
"This loop is the tree. No, that's the ear. Ugh, give it here."
"Apa, I want to do it!"
"Fine. Make one loop."
"Like this?"
"Too big. Why are you so slow? You're six!"
Simran's lip wobbled. "You said bunny ear."
Hafsa stopped. She looked at her own shoe and tied it slowly, watching her fingers. "Okay. Wait. I don't even do bunny ears. I make one loop, wrap the other lace round it, and push it through the hole underneath. Three steps."
"One: loop. Two: wrap. Three: push."
Simran tried. The bow came out lopsided, but it held.
"I did it!"
"You did," Hafsa said, a bit surprised at herself. "Sorry I said slow."

qa.q: How many steps did Hafsa say it takes?
qa.a: Three steps.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when she had to stop and look at her own shoe?
qa.a: Hafsa was impatient at first, then surprised to discover she didn't tie laces the way she was explaining, and a little sorry for snapping.

qa.q: What made Hafsa's second explanation better than the first?
qa.a: She watched how she really did it and broke it into three simple steps, instead of confusing talk about bunny ears and trees.

qa.q: What was it like for Simran to be called slow?
qa.a: Simran felt hurt, with a wobbling lip, but was proud and delighted once the lopsided bow held.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching a younger sibling with both bossiness and real help, and having to organise her own understanding to explain it.
